nameStory: Rock crane's-bill gets its name from two key features: it loves growing in rocky places, and its seed pods look remarkably like a crane's long, pointed beak! When the seeds are ripe, these 'beaks' split open dramatically, flinging seeds in all directions. The 'bigroot' part of its alternate name refers to its thick, sturdy underground rhizomes that help it anchor into rocky crevices.
description: Rock crane's-bill is a low-growing perennial that forms dense, spreading mats about 8-12 inches tall. It has deeply divided, hand-shaped leaves that release a distinctive spicy-sweet fragrance when you brush against them or crush them between your fingers. In early summer, it produces clusters of five-petaled flowers in shades of pale pink to magenta that seem to glow against the aromatic foliage. Originally from the mountains of southeastern Europe, it's now a popular garden escape that occasionally naturalizes in New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into five finger-like lobes (palmate), with a distinctive spicy-sweet scent when crushed - almost like a mix of rose geranium and mint

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five-petaled flowers in pale pink to bright magenta, about 1 inch across, with prominent veining and long stamens extending beyond the petals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading mats through underground rhizomes, staying low at 8-12 inches but spreading widely as groundcover

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive 'crane's bill' seed pods that split explosively when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop'

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, somewhat succulent feeling stems that are often reddish-tinged and covered with soft, sticky hairs

habitat: In New England, rock crane's-bill is primarily found as a garden escape in disturbed areas near homes, old foundations, and abandoned gardens. It occasionally naturalizes in rocky slopes, stone walls, and well-drained woodland edges where it can establish its spreading root system. Look for it in partially shaded spots with good drainage, especially where it has room to spread into a colony.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, forming fresh green mounds with that characteristic spicy fragrance becoming more noticeable as weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with clusters of pink flowers from June through July, followed by the formation of the distinctive crane's-bill seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Leaves often turn brilliant orange-red before dying back, and you might hear the 'pop' of exploding seed pods on warm, dry days.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground rhizomes, leaving dried stems and empty seed pods that persist through snow.

funFact: Rock crane's-bill's seed pods are nature's catapults - when ripe, they can launch seeds up to 20 feet away with such force that you can actually hear them 'pop' on quiet summer days, and the seeds can hit you if you're standing nearby!
confusionNotes: Don't confuse this with our native wild geranium, which has more deeply cut, less fragrant leaves and grows taller in woodland settings. Rock crane's-bill stays low and mat-forming, and that distinctive spicy scent when you touch the leaves is a dead giveaway - wild geranium leaves don't smell nearly as strong.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'geranium,' this isn't the same as the bright red geraniums in window boxes - those are actually Pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like rock crane's-bill are the wild cousins with more delicate flowers and that explosive seed-shooting trick that gave the whole family its 'crane's-bill' nickname.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage. Wild geranium grows 1-2 feet tall in woodlands, while Herb Robert has much more finely divided, fern-like leaves with a different, somewhat unpleasant odor. Rock crane's-bill's thick, spreading growth habit and sweet-spicy fragrance make it unmistakable once you know what to sniff for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
